title: Position- and Temperature-Dependent Responsivity in a KID-Based Phonon-Mediated Detector
authors: Z. J. Smith, O. Wen, S. Q. Dang, E. Panner, J. Anczarski, T. Aralis, T. Dyson, S. W. Henderson, H. Magoon, A. Simchony, C. Stone-Whitehead, N. Tabassum, B. A. Young, M. Munaf, D. J. Temples, C. Cap, C. L. Chang, Y. -Y. Chang, M. Garcia-Sciveres, W. Ho, K. Li, X. Li, R. Linehan, M. Lisovenko, K. Okubo, Manabputra, K. Ramanathan, S. Ray, B. Sandoval, A. Suzuki, G. Wang, M. Williams, J. R. Xiong, V. Yefremenko, B. L. T. Plourde, S. R. Golwala, K. Stifter, N. A. Kurinsky
abstract: We report on the position- and temperature-dependent response of a kinetic inductance phonon-mediated (KIPM) detector. To study position-dependence, we used a controllable mirror attached to a micro-electromechanical system (MEMS) to steer optical light with a 100 $μ$m spot size over the backside of the cryogenic detector. With both pulsed and continuous operation of the LED, we observe features of the detector housing and find that the signal is strongest when the LED is pointed directly at the KID. The "off-KID" response is measured to be 34% of the "on-KID" response and is largely independent of direction. We model phonon propagation and collection in the KIPM detector with G4CMP and assert that the isotropic angular dependence is unlikely to be due to discrete phonon absorption "sinks", such as the microwave feedline or the device mounting points, but can be explained instead by an isotropic energy loss in the crystal. We furthermore utilize the temperature flexibility of the MEMS and KIPM detector system to investigate temperature-dependent responsivity, both at the sensor level (i.e., frequency shifts in the KID) and at the detector level (i.e., position dependence). We fit the KID's response to a two-component heat capacity and present the model as an alternative way to understand the KID's response to absorbed energy. We show on- and off-KID data at a range of temperatures and show that the phonon dynamics are not temperature dependent. We comment on the resulting implication for KID dynamics and design improvements.
summary: This work characterizes a phonon-mediated detector by measuring its response across varying positions and temperatures. The authors establish that the detector's phonon collection efficiency is remarkably stable and isotropic, suggesting bulk energy loss rather than localized defects. By modeling the thermal response using heat capacity components, they provide a comprehensive understanding of the underlying energy dissipation mechanisms.
main_problem: The study investigates the position- and temperature-dependent responsivity of a Kinetic Inductance Phonon-Mediated (KIPM) detector.
main_result: The phonon collection efficiency was found to be largely isotropic and independent of temperature, suggesting energy loss within the crystal rather than discrete absorption sinks.
method: The authors combine MEMS-based optical scanning for position dependence with temperature tuning and fitting the detector response to multi-component heat capacity models.
model_or_system: The system is a KID-based detector coupled to a niobium coplanar waveguide, where phonon transport and energy loss are modeled using G4CMP simulations and analyzed via thermal response fitting.
key_observables: Phonon collection efficiency ($\epsilon_{ph}$), detector response $S_{21}(t; f_r)$, and temperature-dependent heat capacity components ($C_{pb}, C_{Sch}, C_{abs}$).
important_parameters: Temperature range (down to cryogenic levels), optical spot size (100 $\mu$m), and characteristic energy scales like $E_{TLS}/h = 1.2 	ext{ GHz}$.
main_assumptions: The isotropic angular dependence is attributed to isotropic energy loss in the crystal, and the temperature dependence of phonon dynamics is assumed to be negligible.
figures_summary: Figures show the MEMS setup for optical scanning, pulse response measurements (L-scan/V-scan), and detailed fits of the total thermal response ($\Delta T$) to a sum of pair-breaking, Schottky, and absolute capacity components.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from characterizing position dependence using optical scanning, to modeling phonon collection efficiency, and finally to analyzing the temperature dependence by fitting the response to a multi-component heat capacity model.
why_interesting: The detailed analysis of thermal response using heat capacity models and the investigation of energy loss mechanisms provide insights into non-equilibrium thermal dynamics in superconducting circuits, relevant to quantum energy harvesting.
